chapter: Whiteman at the St. Charles Theater
title: Meeting Bix with the Whiteman Orchestra at the St. Charles Theater
summary: Hug tells the story of Whiteman's show, Bix's solos, and the jam at Paul Mares's home.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Before, I'm going to ask you to play a few things on the piano. Yeah. Because I think it shows the kind of thing you've been talking about with the piano and the cornet. But could you just relate the meeting with the Whiteman Orchestra at the St. Charles Theater? Yes. And I think it's an interesting story.

Well, I think it was probably one of the most exciting things that I can remember happening in my musical career. I don't know of any, I've had quite a few nice things happen, but this probably had to be one of the most exciting because, as I say, Bix was, well, it was a magic word at that time. And when we found out that Paul Whiteman was going to tour down this way and he was going to be at the St. Charles Theater, which is no longer here now, they tour it now. Why? This was something that everybody just looked forward to. And, of course, my friend Eddie Miller and Dan LeBlanc was a fine musician. Angelo Palmezana, we were all playing in a band together at the time. We all decided we would go there and hear him, you know. Well, the first half of the performance was confined to a lot of Whiteman's usual arrangements, you know, the big stuff, the heavy, it was the heavy stuff, which was beautiful, you know. He played, he had a beautiful band and beautiful orchestra. And he was playing off some of Gushman's things, you know. And Roy Boy, Roy Boy here at the piano, you know. It was really great. Well, when the intermission came, we went downstairs. And by the time we got down there, well, the musicians had come out into the alleyway. And it was a nice day, nice, brisk day. And, oh, I walked up there and I couldn't believe it. There was Bix standing out there, you know. Bix and Trombau. Paul Merez from the Rhythm Kings, you know. And I just don't recall, like, who else was standing out there. It was Eddie Bell and myself and all of us. We walked up there, you know. We got right in on the con. We walked right into the conversation, you know. And, well, you just sort of felt yourself being taken up, you know. I mean, you were beginning to just be enchanted with what was going on, you know. I mean, just the mere fact that you were standing in the presence of this man and the other people. So, Monk Hazel was with us. And, of course, as I said, dear old Monk, he was always a good old character, you know. You could leave it to him to come up with something real good, you know. So, Bix asked about Leon Rapola. He asked Paul Merez. How was Leon Rapola doing well, you see. It showed that he had a concern for a musician of Rapola's ability, you see. And he asked about a few other musicians. Paul Merez told him, you know, how they were doing. And, well, of course, we stood up there and we were talking a few minutes. Well, here comes Whiteman, who I always admired. I like that big fat fella that he was, you know, with the big round face, you know. He'd come walking in. So, Monk Hazel turned around and saw him walking in. And Monk Hazel goes over to him and says, hey, Paul, wait a minute. I want to see you a minute. So, Paul turned around and he says, Paul, listen. He says, boy, you got all these New Orleans guys here waiting to hear Bix play it. He says, if you don't let him start playing in the next go around, he says, they're going to tear the place down. So, Paul says, oh, yeah. He says, I'm going to let him go. He says, he's going to play it. So, that was that. And then Paul Merez invited Bix and a couple of the other musicians out there. He's out home full of some cocktails and some adores, I guess, some lunch, you know. So, he invited me and Eddie Miller and Monk Hazel and a couple of the other New Orleans boys, which I thought was very nice of him. And...

come out there too. So we went back into the theater and when Mike Whiteman got finished playing Concerto O'NF by Gershwin, he put his baton on and he says, well, he says, all I can say is now, he says, I think I better turn it over to Bix and let him take over. He says, oh, they're going to tear this place down.
Do you remember what they, what did they do?

He started off with Dinah, you mean the tune? Oh, he started, yeah, the tunes. That was the first tune he played was Dinah and I think he played singing the blues if I'm not mistaken. He played about three tunes, you know, and I'm telling you that was really something to hear, you know. And the way the audience received it, you know, boy, they just, it just electrified. They were really, really taken up with it.
Were the numbers much longer than you hear on the records? Because usually records are limited to three minutes or something like that.

Oh, yeah, yes, oh, yes. I guess, I guess he stood up and maybe took about three or four, three or four solos one behind the other, you know. Trombaar took about three or four. Clarinet player would take about three or four, you know. Piano, banjo, they'd pass it around just like they, just like they do today, you know.
And that was longer than you hear on the records.
Oh, much longer than you hear on the records, sure.

I'm sure that he gave them about a 15, 20 minute spot. Oh, boy. Which was a great, which was a great spot. And then that, after that, that's when we went out to Paul Merez's home. And that's when we really got something real going there, you know, with Bix playing the trumpet, you know. And had Izzy Friedman playing clarinet. Snoozer Quinn, one of the real greats, all-time greats. And, well, I said Eddie Miller and, well, they had, that was the local boys, you know. And I can't think, they had some of the other musicians of Whiteman's band, but I can't recall who they were right now. But it was, it was a most memorable experience. And like I say, after Bix showing me some things, I asked him about Intermiss, you know, and he started showing me some, some things on the piano. He says, oh, I can't get them. He says, oh, he says, you don't really find that too hard, let me show you, you know. He says, it's very simple, you know. It's so simple that, you know, you just have to sit there and try to figure out what those chords were, you know. Of course, when he sat down there and played them, it sounded like it was simple, you know.
